claims.text: A surface-enriched manganese layer on Q235 steel preferentially oxidizes.
Preferential manganese oxidation forms a continuous Mn-oxide passivation film.
The Mn-oxide film buffers the corrosive environment and suppresses iron oxidation.
Absence or disruption of the Mn-oxide layer causes uncontrolled iron oxidation and rapid corrosion.
Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a standard low-level manganese content and a native, non-uniform oxide film.
Controlled manganese deposition or annealing in a manganese-rich atmosphere can enrich the near-surface manganese concentration of Q235 steel.
The proposed mediator is a coherent, adherent surface layer of MnO or Mn2O3.
Manganese oxidation has a lower Gibbs free energy than iron oxidation under the proposed exposure conditions.
Surface-enriched manganese rapidly oxidizes in the harsh chloride-rich environment.
Sacrificial manganese oxidation creates a redox buffer that stabilizes surface potential.
Stabilization of surface potential suppresses iron dissolution and slows overall corrosion.
Manganese-enriched samples will form a more uniform and protective Mn-oxide layer than untreated Q235 steel.
Manganese-enriched samples will have significantly lower mass loss and better corrosion resistance than untreated Q235 steel.
The protective effect of manganese enrichment is likely to be more pronounced at approximately 100 °C than at approximately 25 °C.
Untreated Q235 steel will form a thinner, less uniform oxide film that inadequately prevents iron oxidation and therefore corrodes faster.
The protective effect requires environmental conditions that permit formation and retention of the oxide layer.
Excessive chloride exposure or mechanical damage to the oxide layer may eliminate the protective benefit.
The optimal manganese concentration and oxide thickness for passivating Q235 steel are not known precisely.
The controlled comparison uses manganese-enriched and untreated Q235 specimens exposed to the same chloride-rich humid environment at approximately 25 °C and 100 °C.

Failure of manganese enrichment to produce statistically significant improvements in mass loss, oxide uniformity, and electrochemical performance at both temperatures is designated as falsifying the hypothesis.
